These include AWS Organizations SCPs and RCPs,\\\\n resource-based policies, identity-based policies, IAM permissions boundaries, and\\\\n session policies. In all those policies, the enforcement code looks for a\\\\n `Deny` statement that applies to the request. This is called an explicit deny. If the enforcement code finds even one explicit deny that\\\\n applies, the enforcement code returns a final decision of **Deny**. Review the following policy types for explicit **Deny** statements that might block access:\\\\n\\\\n* Identity-based policies\\\\n* Service Control Policies (SCPs)\\\\n* Permissions boundaries\\\\n* Resource-based policies\\\\n\\\\nFor more information about policy evaluation logic, see [Policy evaluation logic](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/troubleshoot-iam-tag-based-access-denied\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Enhanced access denied error messages with policy ARNs | AWS Security Blog\",\"context\":\"### What changed?\\\\n\\\\nWe added the policy ARN to access denied error messages for AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and AWS Organizations policies. {"id": "55f31af9-ce99-4d9a-bcc2-eadd0ceedbe7", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Good, this confirms the current evaluation order. Here's the authorization chain I'd walk for an AI/ML access-denied error (e.g., Bedrock, SageMaker), in the order AWS's enforcement logic actually checks it:

**1. Explicit deny — across every policy type, checked first**
A single explicit `Deny` anywhere below overrides any `Allow`. Check in this order, since AWS now surfaces the exact policy ARN in the error message:
- Service Control Policies (SCPs) — org-wide guardrails
- Resource Control Policies (RCPs) — newer org-wide resource-side guardrails (e.g., can restrict Bedrock/SageMaker resource access regardless of identity policy)
- Resource-based policies (model/endpoint resource policy, S3 bucket policy for training data, KMS key policy)
- Identity-based policies (the user/role's attached policies)
- Permission boundaries
- Session policies (passed with `AssumeRole`/STS)

If any of these has a matching `Deny`, you're done — that's the denial, and the enhanced error message now names the exact policy ARN, so start there before manually walking anything.

**2. RCP allow check** — if no explicit deny, AWS checks whether an RCP permits the request. No applicable `Allow` in RCP → deny.

**3. SCP allow check** — same logic for SCPs if in an AWS Organization.

**4. Resource-based policy allow (or identity-based, for same-account requests)** — standard IAM evaluation: for same-account requests either an identity-based or resource-based `Allow` is sufficient; for cross-account requests, both the resource-based policy on the resource AND the identity-based policy (or a role trust policy via `AssumeRole`) must allow it.

**5. Permission boundary check** — the effective permission is the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary.

**6. Session policy check** — further intersects with whatever was passed at `AssumeRole` time.

For AI/ML specifically, I'd also layer in two service-specific things that aren't generic IAM but produce "access denied"-looking errors:
- **Model/feature access gates** — e.g., Bedrock foundation model access must be explicitly enabled per model in the account/region, separate from IAM.
- **Network path** — VPC endpoint policies and security groups if the call is going over PrivateLink (common for SageMaker).

Want me to pull the specific policies for an account/role and walk this chain against a real denied call you're seeing?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
